climbing_route.label: First major slab (~2,900 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Two low-5th-class pitches following intersecting dikes; parties either solo them or rope up depending on comfort. Exit onto dirt and heather above the slab's upper-left edge. Attempt only bone dry — the slabs and dirt gullies are treacherous wet.

climbing_route.label: Tiny notch, razorback and glade saddle
climbing_route.notes: Route-finding turns serious above the slab: only an intermittent boot path, cairns and flagging lead through a small notch and a knife-edge 'razorback' to the flat 'glade saddle,' a bivy site where many parties split the day.

climbing_route.label: Wooded ramp and ledge traverse to the Y Notch
climbing_route.notes: A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20-ft scramble step, then the usual rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse that leads into the Y Notch.

climbing_route.label: '#2 Gully' to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the Y Notch the route joins the gully system known locally as '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished and mossy rock on the other — for roughly the final 600 ft of short technical pitches to the summit ridge and the 5,519 ft high point.

climbing_route.label: South ridge / summit tower
climbing_route.notes: Gained off unmarked cross-country ground above Iron Cap Lake basin; loose rock and dirt underfoot with occasional steep heather. Class 2-3 scrambling toward the 6,347 ft summit.

climbing_route.label: Downclimb into the notch
climbing_route.notes: From the ridge a short 3rd-class downclimb drops into a notch.

climbing_route.label: Ramp below the summit block to the north ridge
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the notch a wide ramp traverses below the summit block — no sidehilling required — to meet the broad north ridge, which is easy red-rock and dirt scrambling to the true summit.

climbing_route.label: Slinged boulder and left-slanting ramp
climbing_route.notes: A landmark 'slinged boulder' west of camp, reached across steep scree and dirt below the south face, marks the start; from it find a left-slanting ramp that breaches the lower cliff band. Locating this ramp/chimney system on the face is a significant route-finding difficulty.

climbing_route.label: Lower cliff-band step
climbing_route.notes: A short Class 4 step above the ramp.

climbing_route.label: Hidden chimney
climbing_route.notes: The step leads into a hidden Class 3 chimney — hidden being the point, it is easy to miss from below.

climbing_route.label: Upper face to the southeast ridge and summit block
climbing_route.notes: Roughly 1,000 ft of Class 2-3 scrambling above the chimney, including a stretch of exposed low-5th-class climbing with two informal belay stations reported near 8,000 ft, gains the southeast ridge and the summit block. Loose rock throughout.

climbing_route.label: South ridge flank above Headlee Pass
climbing_route.notes: Leave the trail at the pass (~4,600 ft) and work generally north along and below Morning Star's south ridge over talus, heather benches and progressively steeper rock and gully terrain. This is a genuine T5/S4 scramble — sustained exposed class 3 with sections bordering class 4 — not a hike.

climbing_route.label: Steep gully / rock rib
climbing_route.notes: A steep gully partway up is often icy; parties commonly move onto the rock rib to its right to avoid the ice. Loose blocks.

climbing_route.label: Upper scramble to the summit (6,020 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Route-finding gets progressively harder the higher you go and cairns mark only parts of the line. Treat the last mile of scrambling as the technical crux of the day; not for parties uneasy on exposed class 3-4 or in poor visibility.

climbing_route.label: Bowl below the summit block
climbing_route.notes: From One Acre Lake work up and around to the base of the prominent summit block, aiming for the bowl directly beneath it. In winter and spring at least one avalanche-prone slope below this bowl must be crossed — one party reported watching roughly 20 slides release nearby in a single outing, so avoid the line during or after a storm cycle and in rapid warming.

climbing_route.label: Steep gully to the notch below the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: A steep slope/gully leads from the bowl to the notch just under the summit ridge: dirt, talus, and snow in early season. Once it melts out in mid-to-late summer the gully turns genuinely difficult — muddy, loose and exposed.

climbing_route.label: Dome-Sinister col (7,640')
climbing_route.notes: Reached by traversing right (east) across the Chikamin Glacier from about 7,200'. A bergschrund at the col can be hard to cross late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it — the same feature is met again on the way out.

climbing_route.label: Snowfield and south-side gully to the upper west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the col contour an easy snowfield, then climb a loose, unpleasant gully on Sinister's south side to gain the upper west ridge. Loose rock in this gully is the main climbing-specific hazard. Some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col instead.

climbing_route.label: Upper west ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Class 2-3 scrambling along the ridge to the 8,444' summit.
